X32: Drums on One Fader

Assign every miked piece of a drum kit to one DCA fader, and make a mute group that silences the whole kit with one button.

A miked drum kit takes up eight or nine channels. During a show you want to turn the whole kit up or down with one hand, and mute it with one button. The X32 has two tools for this:

Tool What it does How many
DCA group One fader that moves the level of every channel assigned to it 8 (DCA 1–8)
Mute group One button that mutes every channel assigned to it 6 (Mute Group 1–6)

Page numbers below are the PDF pages of the Behringer X32 Preliminary User Manual (links in Works Cited).

Before you start: a channel plan

Plug the drum mics into neighbouring channels and name them. A typical kit:

Ch Mic Name on the scribble strip
1 Kick (inside) KICK IN
2 Kick (outside) KICK OUT
3 Snare top SNARE T
4 Snare bottom SNARE B
5 Hi-hat HAT
6 Rack tom TOM 1
7 Floor tom TOM 2
8 Overhead left OH L
9 Overhead right OH R

Your kit may have fewer mics; the steps are the same. Set each drum’s gain, low cut, gate and EQ first (Live Sound lessons 2–5) and get a rough balance between them on their own faders. The DCA then moves that balance up and down as one.

DCA or group bus?

A DCA (digitally controlled amplifier) does not mix the drums into a new signal. It just moves every assigned channel’s level at once, so each drum still has its own fader for small fixes (manual p. 32).

A group is a mix bus that the channels feed at unity gain: the drums really are summed into one signal. Use one when you want to process the whole kit together, for example one compressor across all the drums, which “would not be possible with a DCA group” (manual p. 32–33). For one fader to ride the kit during a show, use a DCA. You can use both.

Overheads on a noisy stage

The overheads (channels 8 and 9) are the hardest mics on the kit. They hang over the cymbals, a long way from any drum, so they also hear the guitar amps, the bass rig, the wedges and the singer. On a loud stage that bleed can make up more of their signal than the drums do. Push the DRUMS DCA up and the whole band gets louder with it.

Use directional mics. Use cardioid or hypercardioid overheads, not omnis. With hypercardioids, watch for “hot spots” when they point straight down (La Cerra). Omnis only work set low and close over the kit.

Pick a height. La Cerra’s starting point is “approximately six feet high, pointing either straight down to the floor or angled toward the center of the kit.” Higher gives a more even blend of the cymbals. Lower and closer gives more drum and less stage. On a noisy stage, start low, just above the cymbals’ reach, and raise them only as far as the blend needs.

Aim the dead side at the noise. A cardioid hears least from directly behind. Angling the overheads slightly toward the audience “increase[s] rejection of the drum monitors” (La Cerra). Do the same for a guitar amp or a wedge that sits close to the kit: turn the back of the mic toward it.

Keep them in step. Two mics at different distances from the snare cause phase trouble (thin, hollow drums). Measure from the centre of the snare to each overhead and make the two distances equal. Then press the X32’s mono button in the monitor section and listen: if the kit goes thin when both are up, move one mic. The 3:1 rule (mics at least three times as far from each other as from their source) is a rough guide for spaced mics often quoted by engineers (unverified: no source checked yet).

Clean them up on the console.

  • Low cut high. The kick and toms have their own mics, so the overheads only need cymbals and some snare. Try 150–300 Hz; the X32 goes up to 400 Hz (Maillot p. 26).
  • No gate. Cymbals ring for a long time and a gate chops them off (Live Sound 4).
  • Less fader. In a small, loud room the cymbals carry on their own. Bring the overheads up only until the cymbals sit right in the PA. Sometimes the right level is very low, or one overhead, or none.

Turn the stage down. No mic choice fixes everything. Ask the guitarist to point the amp away from the kit or turn it down. Turn down the drummer’s wedge, or fill it with less of everything else. A quieter stage helps every mic, not only the overheads.

Make the DCA

  1. On the right-hand fader section, press GROUP DCA 1-8 so the eight faders there are DCAs (p. 16, 32).
  2. Hold the Select button of DCA 1.
  3. While holding it, press Select on every drum channel: 1 through 9. If the channels are on another layer (17–32), switch the left-hand layer while still holding DCA 1’s Select. Inputs, aux channels, FX returns and bus masters can all go in a DCA (p. 32).
  4. Let go. To check, press DCA 1’s Select again: the Select buttons of its channels light up (p. 8, 32).
  5. To take a channel out, hold DCA 1’s Select and press that channel’s Select again (it toggles; not stated in the manual, so check that the light goes off).

Name it. Press SETUP, page right to DCA GROUPS, turn the first encoder to DCA 1 and press it. Pick a colour, an icon and the name DRUMS, then press the sixth encoder to leave (p. 32).

Use it. Leave DCA 1 at 0 dB (unity) while you build the drum balance on the channel faders. In the show, ride DCA 1. Its Mute button mutes the DCA and its Solo solos all its channels (p. 16). Solo on a DCA is PFL unless you choose DCA Group AFL in the monitor’s solo preferences (p. 31).

Monitor mixes. A DCA works by moving channel levels after the fader. Sends to the stage monitors that are set pre-fader should not follow it; post-fader sends (reverb, for example) should. The manual does not spell this out: check it once by watching a monitor bus meter while you move DCA 1.

Make the mute group

A mute group has a safety step so you can’t mute channels by accident while you set it up (p. 8):

  1. Press MUTE GRP next to the main screen. The screen shows the mute group view, and the channel Mute buttons stop muting while you assign (p. 32, 59).
  2. Hold Mute Group button 1 (bottom right of the console, beside the Main LR fader).
  3. While holding it, press Select on drum channels 1–9 (any layer, inputs or outputs) (p. 59).
  4. Let go, and press MUTE GRP again. The buttons work normally again (p. 32).
  5. Press Mute Group 1 to mute the whole kit; press it again to bring it back (p. 32).

Good uses: mute the drums between songs or while the drummer is setting up; put the drum reverb return in the same mute group so the reverb tail mutes too.

Mute Group 1 mutes the drums wherever they go. Muting DCA 1 does the same job from the DCA fader. Pick one and tell the other people who run the board, so nobody wonders why the drums won’t come back.

Save it

Store a scene once it works (the Scenes buttons, p. 17). The DCA names and assignments live in the console’s setup, and the manual says DCA group settings “are stored with the Scene data” (p. 28). Load the scene at the start of the next rehearsal, and press DCA 1’s Select to check the drums are still in it.

If it doesn’t work

Problem Check
Pressing channel Selects just selects them You let go of the DCA’s (or mute group’s) button too soon. Hold it the whole time.
The faders on the right are buses, not DCAs Press GROUP DCA 1-8 (p. 16).
Mute group buttons mute nothing MUTE GRP is still on (assign mode). Press it again (p. 32).
Drums silent and nothing looks muted Check DCA 1’s Mute and Mute Group 1. Both can mute the kit.
The drum balance changed Someone moved a channel fader. The DCA keeps the channels’ balance; it doesn’t store it.

For the curious: what the console stores

In Maillot’s OSC reference, each channel keeps its groups as two numbers: /ch/01/grp/dca (8 bits, one per DCA) and /ch/01/grp/mute (6 bits, one per mute group) (p. 28). Each DCA has its own on, fader, name, icon and color (p. 39). The Config → Mute System preferences include “Hard Mutes” and “DCA groups” (p. 56); the reference names them but doesn’t say what they do, so leave them alone unless you’ve tested them.

Works Cited

For students

Behringer. X32 Digital Mixer Preliminary User Manual. Music Tribe, media.vsl-uk.com/manuals/sound/Behringer_X32_User_Manual.pdf. Channel strip sections and order, preamps (72 dB range, +23 dBu), set-up steps for a mic, USB 2-track recorder (Aux 7/8), scenes, GEQ effects.

La Cerra, Steve. “Sweet Sounds From the Stage.” Mix, 1 Nov. 2007, www.mixonline.com/live-sound/sweet-sounds-stage-368579. Live drum overheads: about six feet up, directional patterns, hypercardioid hot spots, angling toward the audience to reject the drum monitors.

For teachers

Maillot, Patrick-Gilles. Unofficial X32/M32 OSC Remote Protocol. 2020, tostibroeders.nl/wp-content/uploads/2020/02/X32-OSC.pdf. Ranges of gain, low cut, gate, compressor, EQ and fader; the fader law; Aux In channels have no gate or dynamics.
